newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel business sector divided over Netanyahu.
newsitem.headline: Israel business sector divided over Netanyahu.

text.p: The economic and political policies of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu have divided Israel's business sector, where some applaud his actions while others fear for the future.

On the political front, the future of the Middle East peace process hangs in limbo -- and with it the fate of foreign investment, which soared in the wake of the original 1993 Palestinian-Israeli peace accord.
Some foreign investors continue to display significant interest in the Israeli economy, especially in the telecommunications and export-oriented high-tech sector.

But others have taken a wait-and-see attitude as Palestinian and Israeli negotiators try to advance the peace process, stalled since the right-wing Likud-led government ousted the Labour party from power in May elections.
"The Israeli economy is faced with uncertainty. Declarations are not enough," said Benjamin Gaon, president of Israel's leading concern Koor Industries.

But Gaon sees as positive two recent developments. He believes the government is now close to redeploying troops from the West Bank town of Hebron, one of the thorniest issues in talks with Palestinians.

He also said there has been a warming of relations with Egypt ahead of this week's Middle East economic summit in Cairo. Relations between Israel and its first Arab partner in peace had cooled substantially after Netanyahu took office.
The peace process is not just crucial for foreign investors, analysts say.
Netanyahu will need political stability to deal with a rapidly slowing economy, an expanding budget deficit and declining national savings.

"No country in a situation of political or military tension can open up problems on another front. The peace process is important to the ability to deal with domestic problems as well," said Yoram Gabbay, head of Bank Hapoalim's portfolio management company Peilim.

Gabbay, former director of the state revenue administration, was particularly pessimistic with regard to Netanyahu's ability to carry out a sweeping programme of privatisation and deregulation as he has promised.

"All real privatisation and deregulation means having to deal with power structures like the labour unions," said Gabbay, who believes this will be difficult as long as the government is occupied with political problems.

He praised Netanyahu's proposed 190.8 billion shekel budget for 1997, which includes 4.9 billion shekels in cuts, saying it addresses many problems and would allow the central bank to ease up somewhat on interest rates.

But the original proposal, which the government admits may undergo some changes, calls for more than 800 million shekels in defence cuts. "Political conditions won't allow any (defence) cuts. A compromise will be needed. The government will have to find cuts in other places," Gabbay said.
The ailing Tel Aviv stock market has so far expressed little faith in Netanyahu's policies. The average trading volume in recent weeks has sunk to the lowest level in recent years.
"Netanyahu has done nothing. He is only talking. He spoke about an economic plan but we haven't seen anything," said Amir Eayal, head of portfolio mangement at Epsilon Securities.
But, he added: "The approval of such a plan will change the attitude of investors towards the new Likud-led government."

Yet others like Daniel Carasso, director of Israel research at UBS Securities, believe that given the short period of time in power, the new government has moved quickly on the economic front. Besides launching the ambitious budget proposal, the government last week awarded two licences to operate international phone service in competition with state-controlled monopoly Bezeq.
"If anyone has a chance of doing what needs to be done, like reducing the budget deficit, this is a government that can do it," Carasso said.
($1 = 3.25 shekels)
